records.source: Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS), Bitol, LF AI and Data Foundation
records.version_or_commit: v3.1.0; 607 commits on main; media type application/odcs+yaml;version=3.1.0
records.finding: A data contract is a single machine-readable document covering schema, quality rules, service levels, owning team and support channel together. Splitting those into separate artefacts is what lets a table keep its schema while quietly losing its freshness guarantee, because nobody owns the gap between them.
records.applicability_limits: A document format, not an enforcement engine: nothing in the standard runs the quality rules or measures the service level, and adoption outside the Bitol tool circle is still small. The pricing and infrastructure sections are aimed at inter-company data sharing and are dead weight inside a single venture.
records.counter_evidence: Competing formats exist (the Open Data Product Specification, vendor-native contract schemas in dbt), so committing to ODCS is a bet on a format war that is not settled.

records.source: Schelter, Lange, Schmidt, Celikel, Biessmann and Grafberger, Automating Large-Scale Data Quality Verification (Deequ)
records.study_design: System description with experimental evaluation on several datasets at Amazon
records.population: Production data pipelines at a large online retailer
records.benchmark: Internal datasets; incremental metric computation and anomaly detection experiments
records.licence: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (stated on the paper); paraphrase only, no reuse of wording
records.finding: Data quality checks are declarative constraints compiled into aggregation queries, so the check runs as part of the pipeline rather than as a separate audit. Two mechanisms matter beyond assertions: incremental computation of metrics over growing datasets, so the cost does not scale with history, and anomaly detection over the time series of past metric values, which catches drift that no fixed threshold was written for.
records.applicability_limits: Built for Spark-scale batch data at a retailer; the incremental machinery is unnecessary below a few million rows, where a full rescan is cheaper than the state it saves. Constraint suggestion learns from the data as it is, so it will happily suggest a rule that encodes a current bug as the norm.
records.counter_evidence: The paper's own framing (unit tests for data) presumes the producer knows the invariants. The anomaly-detection path exists precisely because that presumption fails, which is an admission that declared-rule approaches such as dbt contracts do not cover the failure that actually bites.

records.source: dbt Labs, How we structure our dbt projects
records.licence: unknown (no licence statement on the page)
records.finding: Layer transformations by how far they have travelled from the source, not by subject: staging models are one-to-one with source tables and do only cleaning and renaming, intermediate models hold the joins and logic, and marts are wide business entities. The value is that a naming prefix tells you what a model is allowed to do, so review is mechanical.
records.applicability_limits: Vendor guidance for one transformation tool, presented as convention with no measurement behind it. The three-layer split adds model count and build time, which is real cost on a small warehouse. It says nothing about dimensional design inside the marts layer.
records.counter_evidence: The recommendation to land on wide business entities sits against Kimball dimensional practice, which keeps facts narrow and joins to conformed dimensions. Both are widely used and the guide does not argue the difference.

records.version_or_commit: page as served 2026-08-03; underlying technique PDF dated 2013-09
records.licence: All rights reserved, The Kimball Group; paraphrase only
records.finding: Three decisions carry dimensional modelling and they are made in order: declare the grain of the fact table first, then the dimensions that apply at that grain, then the facts. Conformed dimensions are the integration mechanism, letting separate fact tables be compared without a central model. The slowly changing dimension types are a numbered menu of history policies (overwrite, new row, new column and hybrids), which turns an argument about history into a choice from a list.
records.applicability_limits: Formalised for on-premises relational warehouses where storage and joins were expensive; the cost argument for surrogate keys and narrow facts is much weaker on columnar cloud storage. The site has not been substantially updated since the Kimball Group wound down, so treat it as a settled body of technique, not a maintained one.
records.counter_evidence: Modern practice frequently lands on wide denormalised marts (see the dbt structure guide) and skips surrogate keys entirely; the grain-first and conformed-dimension arguments survive that shift, the physical prescriptions largely do not.

records.source: Armbrust, Ghodsi, Xin and Zaharia, Lakehouse: A New Generation of Open Platforms that Unify Data Warehousing and Advanced Analytics
records.study_design: Position paper with a TPC-DS performance comparison against cloud data warehouses
records.licence: unknown (no licence statement on the paper)
records.finding: The failure mode of the two-tier lake-plus-warehouse shape is not performance, it is that the same facts exist twice with an ETL hop between them, producing staleness, reliability gaps and duplicated cost. The argued fix is one copy in an open direct-access format with a metadata layer over it giving transactions and schema enforcement, and the paper reports TPC-DS results competitive with cloud warehouses to show the performance objection is answerable.
records.applicability_limits: Written by the vendor whose product is the lakehouse, so the architectural claim and the commercial interest coincide. TPC-DS is a synthetic decision-support benchmark and does not represent interactive product analytics. The argument presumes machine learning and unstructured data are in scope; for a venture doing SQL over structured events, the second-generation problem it solves may never arise.
records.counter_evidence: Directly contradicted on scale grounds by Tigani's account of BigQuery workloads, where most customers hold under a terabyte and most queries scan under 100 MB, at which point the two-tier problem the lakehouse solves does not exist because there is no lake.

records.version_or_commit: unknown exact release; main branch at 8,992 commits, inspected 2026-08-03; format specification versioned separately
records.finding: An open table format is the seam that stops a warehouse choice from becoming a data lock-in: the table metadata (snapshots, schema evolution, partition evolution) lives with the files, so Spark, Trino, Flink and others read the same table without an export. Buying a query engine and owning your table format are separable decisions.
records.applicability_limits: Catalogue operation, compaction and snapshot expiry are ongoing maintenance work that a managed warehouse does for you; below a few terabytes that overhead usually exceeds the lock-in it avoids. The format specification and the Java implementation move at different speeds from the Python, Go and Rust implementations, so multi-engine parity is a claim to verify per feature, not a given.

records.source: Jordan Tigani, Big Data is Dead (MotherDuck blog)
records.study_design: Practitioner account of internal BigQuery telemetry; figures recalled, not published
records.finding: Storage size and working set are different quantities and only the second sets the architecture. From BigQuery experience the author reports most customers holding under a terabyte in total and around ninety per cent of queries scanning under 100 MB, a power-law distribution in which even large enterprises mostly run small queries. The decision rule that follows: size the analytics stack to the query working set, and treat distributed processing as something to justify, not assume.
records.applicability_limits: Vendor commentary from a single-node warehouse company, and the author states the figures are from memory with the charts hand-drawn, so the numbers are indicative rather than measurements you can cite as data. Nothing here addresses streaming, unstructured data or machine-learning training sets.
records.counter_evidence: The lakehouse position paper argues the opposite direction of travel, that dataset growth and unstructured data broke the warehouse shape. Both cannot be the default; the disagreement is about which population you belong to.

records.source: Johari, Pekelis and Walsh, Always Valid Inference: Continuous Monitoring of A/B Tests
records.study_design: Statistical methodology with deployment on a commercial experimentation platform
records.population: Hundreds of thousands of commercial A/B tests
records.version_or_commit: arXiv:1512.04922v3, 16 July 2019; published in Operations Research
records.licence: unknown (arXiv listing; no explicit reuse licence recorded)
records.finding: Peeking is a property of the stopping rule, not of the operator's discipline, so the fix belongs in the statistic rather than in a policy telling people not to look. Always-valid p-values and confidence intervals, built on a mixture sequential probability ratio test, stay valid at every moment, which makes continuous monitoring a supported operation instead of a violation.
records.applicability_limits: Validity at all times is bought with power: for a fixed effect size a sequential test needs more samples than a correctly powered fixed-horizon test that is genuinely left alone until the end. The method assumes a single pre-declared metric and a stable randomisation unit, and it does not address multiple metrics or multiple variants.
records.counter_evidence: Kohavi, Deng and Vermeer treat peeking as a misunderstanding to be corrected rather than a workflow to be supported; the two positions differ on whether the operator or the statistic should change.

records.source: Kohavi, Deng and Vermeer, A/B Testing Intuition Busters: Common Misunderstandings in Online Controlled Experiments
records.study_design: Synthesis of practitioner errors with statistical argument, drawn from experimentation platforms at several large firms
records.population: Online controlled experiments at web-scale companies
records.finding: The dominant experimentation errors are interpretive, not computational: reading a p-value as the probability the result is chance, monitoring continuously with a fixed-horizon test (which can push the type I error rate far above the nominal five per cent), ignoring sample ratio mismatch, and forgetting that with roughly eighty-five to ninety per cent of ideas failing to move the target metric, the prior is against you and a bare significant result is more likely false than a naive reading suggests. Twyman's law follows: a surprisingly large effect is evidence of a bug before it is evidence of a win.
records.applicability_limits: Written from platforms running hundreds of concurrent experiments with millions of users; the low success base rate is measured on mature products where the obvious wins are gone, and an early-stage venture testing crude changes may face a different prior. It offers no method for a venture that cannot reach the sample size for a properly powered test at all.
records.counter_evidence: Its anti-peeking stance is answered by always-valid and group-sequential methods, which make monitoring legitimate rather than forbidden.

records.source: Kohavi, Deng, Frasca, Walker, Xu and Pohlmann, Online Controlled Experiments at Large Scale
records.study_design: Experience report on the Bing experimentation system
records.population: Over 200 concurrent experiments per day at Bing
records.licence: unknown (ACM proceedings; author copy served by exp-platform.com)
records.finding: At scale the binding constraint is trustworthiness, not throughput. Two mechanisms carry it: alerting rather than up-front testing, because the number of live variants makes exhaustive pre-release testing impossible, and explicit detection of interactions between concurrently running experiments. The report also defends deliberately running experiments expected to degrade the experience, on the grounds that the size of the loss is the only way to price the feature.
records.applicability_limits: Everything here presumes traffic that a small venture does not have; with one experiment at a time, interaction detection is moot and alerting has nothing to alert on. Thirteen years old, and the platform economics have changed.

records.source: Deng, Xu, Kohavi and Walker, Improving the Sensitivity of Online Controlled Experiments by Utilizing Pre-Experiment Data (CUPED)
records.study_design: Method with evaluation on Bing's production experimentation system
records.licence: ACM copyright 2013, all rights reserved (stated on the paper); paraphrase only
records.finding: Sensitivity is cheaper to buy through variance reduction than through traffic. Using each user's pre-experiment behaviour as a covariate removes the part of the metric that has nothing to do with the treatment, and on Bing this cut variance by roughly half, which is the same power at half the users or half the duration. The precondition is that you already store per-unit history before the experiment starts.
records.applicability_limits: Requires a stable randomisation unit observed before the experiment, so it does nothing for new users, first-session funnels or anonymous traffic. Reported on one search product's metrics; the variance reduction achieved depends entirely on how strongly pre-period behaviour predicts in-period behaviour, and for rare conversion events that correlation can be near zero.

records.source: Fabijan, Gupchup, Gupta, Omhover, Qin, Vermeer and Dmitriev, Diagnosing Sample Ratio Mismatch in Online Controlled Experiments
records.study_design: Taxonomy derived from experiments across four companies and more than twenty-five products
records.population: Online controlled experiments serving hundreds of millions of users
records.finding: A mismatch between the assignment ratio you asked for and the ratio you observed invalidates the experiment outright, because whatever caused the imbalance almost certainly also biased the metric. The paper turns this into a diagnosis procedure by classifying causes into where they arise (assignment, execution, log processing, telemetry, interference), so the check is not just a red light but a search order.
records.applicability_limits: The chi-squared check needs enough units for the ratio deviation to be detectable, so small experiments can pass while badly broken. The taxonomy comes from large platforms with layered assignment services; a venture with one feature flag has fewer places for a mismatch to hide and a correspondingly shorter search.

records.finding: An open library that puts the corrections in the analysis path rather than in a checklist: z and Welch tests, group sequential testing, multiple-comparison correction, variance reduction and non-inferiority margins in one place. The existence of a maintained library at this size shows the statistical machinery is not a reason to buy a platform.
records.applicability_limits: Self-described beta with a small maintainer surface, and it analyses data you have already collected correctly; it cannot fix assignment, logging or sample ratio problems upstream. Choosing between its sequential and fixed-horizon paths is left to the user with no guidance on the power cost.

records.version_or_commit: unknown exact release; master branch inspected 2026-08-03
records.finding: Product analytics events are treated as versioned, resolvable schemas held in a registry, so an event is validated against a published contract at collection time and bad events are quarantined rather than silently landed. SchemaVer separates changes that break consumers from changes that only add, which makes the compatibility question explicit at the point of authoring.
records.applicability_limits: Registry, resolver and validation infrastructure is real operational weight, and it fits a pipeline you control end to end; a venture on a hosted analytics SDK cannot easily insert it. Validation checks structure, not whether the event fires at the right moment or means what the name says.
records.counter_evidence: The lighter convention-only approach (object-action naming plus a shared tracking plan) claims most of the benefit with none of the infrastructure, and no comparison of the two exists in the sources found.

records.source: Twilio Segment, Naming conventions for clean data
records.licence: Copyright Twilio Inc., all rights reserved; paraphrase only
records.finding: Event taxonomy is generated, not enumerated: pick the objects in the product and the actions that can be done to them, and every event name is an object-action pair. The corollary rule is that anything varying per occurrence belongs in a property, never in the event name, which is what stops an event catalogue exploding into thousands of near-duplicates.
records.applicability_limits: Vendor guidance whose enforcement story is that vendor's product, with no evidence beyond assertion. Casing conventions are arbitrary and only consistency matters. The page is silent on who owns the tracking plan and how a change to it is reviewed, which is the part that actually decays.

records.source: NIST SP 800-226, Guidelines for Evaluating Differential Privacy Guarantees
records.finding: A differential privacy claim is only meaningful with its parameters stated, and the guidance frames evaluation as a layered pyramid rather than a single epsilon number. It names privacy hazards, the gaps that open when the mathematics is realised in software, which is the honest way to read any vendor claim of privacy-preserving analytics: ask what the privacy unit is and what the implementation does that the proof does not cover.
records.applicability_limits: Guidance for evaluating differential privacy specifically; it does not tell you whether differential privacy is the right control for your case, and for a small venture the usual answer is that collecting less data is cheaper than noising it. Detail lives in the full document rather than the landing page inspected here.

records.version_or_commit: unknown exact release; main branch inspected 2026-08-03
records.finding: Working differentially private counts, sums, means, variances and quantiles with budget accounting are available as libraries, so the barrier to privacy-preserving aggregate reporting is design, not implementation. The documented limitation is the load-bearing part: the primitives assume each user contributes a bounded number of rows per partition and do not enforce that bound, so contribution limiting is the caller's job and getting it wrong silently voids the guarantee.
records.applicability_limits: Aggregate statistics only; nothing here helps with row-level data sharing or with re-identification risk in an event stream. Correct use requires choosing epsilon and the privacy unit, which the library cannot do for you. Maintainers commit to three months notice before dropping support, which is a short horizon for a dependency in a compliance path.
